findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch without invoking a shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax such as `HEAD; malicious-command`, `exec()` executes the appended command with the application's privileges. Pass the branch as a separate argument using `execFile()` so ref names are not interpreted by a shell.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve ownership of the Git child process
findings.body: For a valid ref containing shell metacharacters such as `foo&`, the shell can exit while Git continues. Consumers then cannot cancel the operation through the returned child's `.kill()`, potentially leaving expensive work running. Spawn Git directly so the returned process remains the operation being controlled.

findings.title: [P2] Restore direct child-process tracking for Git
findings.body:
On POSIX, a valid branch name such as `foo&` is parsed as a background shell command. The returned `ChildProcess` then represents the shell, which can exit before `git show` completes; calling `.kill()` cannot cancel the surviving Git process. This breaks completion and cancellation semantics and may orphan expensive Git operations.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argument instead of interpolating it into a shell command
findings.body:
`exec()` invokes a shell, so input such as `HEAD; <command>` executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. Shell metacharacters are also valid in some Git branch names, making legitimate refs fail or behave unexpectedly.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass branch names without invoking a shell
findings.body:
`exec()` interpolates `branch` into a shell command, enabling arbitrary command execution with the process’s privileges. Any attacker-controlled value containing shell syntax, such as `HEAD; malicious-command`, triggers it on POSIX systems; equivalent metacharacters apply on Windows.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Preserve direct ownership of the Git process
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the shell process rather than the spawned `git` process. If a consumer cancels a slow or large `git show` via the returned child’s `.kill()`, the shell can terminate while Git continues consuming CPU, disk I/O, and memory. The previous `execFile()` implementation killed Git directly.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
